source: CK-12 Life Science Concepts for Middle School, CC-BY-NC
notes: Lesson on genetic information. Structure: hook (genome size) → DNA structure → bases/base pairing → double helix diagram → RNA types → DNA vs RNA comparison → protein synthesis overview → video → practice.

units.label: Hook: human genome facts (text)
units.content_summary: The human genome contains about 3 billion base pairs encoding ~20,000 genes. If uncoiled, the DNA in one cell would stretch 2 metres. Establishes the scale and importance of DNA.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: describe structure of DNA; explain base pairing rules; describe types of RNA and their roles; summarise protein synthesis.

units.label: DNA structure: nucleotide components (text)
units.content_summary: DNA is made of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. Four bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C).

units.label: Nucleotide diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram showing a single nucleotide with deoxyribose sugar, phosphate group, and one of the four bases. Colour-coded: phosphate blue, sugar orange, base varies by type.

units.label: Base pairing rules (text)
units.content_summary: Chargaff's rules: A always pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds); G always pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds). This complementary base pairing is fundamental to DNA replication and transcription.

units.label: Double helix structure diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Classic double helix diagram showing two antiparallel strands twisted around each other, base pairs in the middle (A-T and G-C), sugar-phosphate backbone on outside. Watson-Crick model (1953).

units.label: Video: DNA structure animation (video)
units.content_summary: Animated video showing DNA double helix being unzipped to reveal base pairs, then re-zipped. Demonstrates complementary base pairing dynamically. Narrated with clear labels.

units.label: RNA: types and roles (text)
units.content_summary: Three types of RNA: (1) mRNA (messenger RNA) — carries genetic code from nucleus to ribosome; (2) tRNA (transfer RNA) — brings amino acids to ribosome; (3) rRNA (ribosomal RNA) — structural component of ribosome. RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).

units.label: DNA vs RNA comparison table (image)
units.content_summary: Side-by-side comparison table: DNA vs RNA. Rows: sugar (deoxyribose vs ribose), bases (A,T,G,C vs A,U,G,C), strands (double vs single), location (nucleus vs nucleus+cytoplasm), function (stores info vs carries/uses info).

units.label: Protein synthesis overview: transcription (text)
units.content_summary: Transcription: DNA → mRNA in nucleus. RNA polymerase unzips DNA and builds complementary mRNA strand. mRNA leaves nucleus and travels to ribosome. Key enzyme: RNA polymerase.

units.label: Protein synthesis overview: translation (text)
units.content_summary: Translation: mRNA → protein at ribosome. tRNA reads codons (3-base sequences) on mRNA and brings matching amino acids. Amino acids linked into polypeptide chain = protein.

units.label: Protein synthesis diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram showing nucleus (DNA → mRNA via transcription) connected by arrow to ribosome (mRNA + tRNA → protein via translation). Shows flow of genetic information.

units.label: Practice: base pairing questions (text)
units.content_summary: Five questions: given one strand (e.g. ATGCCA), write the complementary strand; identify base pairs; determine the mRNA sequence transcribed from a DNA template.

units.label: Practice: DNA vs RNA identification (text)
units.content_summary: Four questions asking students to identify whether a description refers to DNA or RNA, and explain which type of RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) is described in each scenario.

units.label: Lesson root: DNA and RNA lesson
